name: Daria Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on a 300-cow dairy farm run by the Brandt family, and we milk with robots, eight of them. The cow walks into a stall when she feels like it, a robot arm finds the teats with a camera and puts the cups on, and she walks out when she's done. So my day isn't milking, it's chasing the cows that didn't go, checking the alerts on the screen, cleaning the units, feeding calves, and scraping out. I start at six and I'm usually finished around five, unless a robot throws an error at two in the morning and the phone goes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you get on with the tech?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love it, honestly, I'm on the herd software and the collar data all day, and I use a chat app to help me read the trends, like which cows are getting mastitis, which is an udder infection. Where I'm weak is the hands-on bit, I'm not great at handling a cow that doesn't want to move, and Josef, the herd manager, is ten times better than me at reading an animal. I share a house in town with Hana, she's a nurse, and we compare night-shift horror stories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's basically our farm already. The robots arrived ten years ago and the world didn't end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People overhype it, but the useful stuff is real and it's already in our sheds. I'd say it plainly, without getting into a big debate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I was hoping for better tools, not fewer jobs, just better ones. If nothing moves, my route up is waiting for Josef to retire, and he's 48. If AI stalls, my career plan is Josef's knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep learning the herd software deeper than anyone else on the farm. Ask the Brandts if I can take over the data side properly, with a small pay rise to go with it. And keep saving, I've got about five months put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the Brandts give you that pay rise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I showed them I'd saved them money, yes. Last year I spotted a cow going lame on the data three days before anyone saw it limping. That's the kind of thing I'd put in front of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said restless. Restless for what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For something that grows. I don't want to scrape out sheds at 40. I'm not sure what I want instead, but I know it's more than this.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because AI was overhyped but the useful parts are real and already on dairy farms. I'd say it plainly without starting a debate.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, because I wanted better tools, not fewer jobs. If nothing moves, my only route up is waiting for the herd manager to retire.
S0.do: Keeps working on the robotic dairy and learns the herd software more deeply than anyone else there. Asks the owners to let her run the data side for a small pay rise, and keeps adding to about five months of savings.
S0.quote: If AI stalls, my career plan is Josef's knees.
S0.fieldNote: Daria already works alongside robots, so the plateau looks to her like the present. She's restless for growth and would be slightly let down if the tools stopped improving. She'd sell her data skills to her employer with concrete examples of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is where dairy's heading anyway, I think. Feed robots, cameras that score the cows' body condition, drones on the grazing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for farms that move early and hard for those that don't. I'd say it to friends who work on older-style farms, too, gently, because some of them are still milking in the old parlours twice a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in a good spot, because I already understand the machines. But I also know the hands-on gap would close, the robots would be better with cows than I am. My edge is the screen, and the screen is getting smarter too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get certified by the robot maker as a service technician, they run a course at the dealer in the next town, about three weeks. Ask the Brandts to pay half. And start to think about working for the dealer instead, going farm to farm fixing robots, because that's where the growth is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. With a small voice saying 'don't get cocky'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Petr, who does the calves. He's brilliant with them, but he won't touch a screen. The cows already work for a robot. Petr's the one who'd struggle to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really leave the Brandts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the dealer paid more and the job had a future, yes. I like the Brandts, but loyalty doesn't pay rent. I'd tell them first, though, and give them proper notice.

S1.say: I'd say this is good for farms that move early and hard for those that don't. I'd gently tell friends still in old-style parlours to get ready.
S1.think: I'm in a good spot because I understand the machines, but robots would soon handle cows better than me. My edge is the screen, and the screen is getting smarter too.
S1.do: Takes a three-week service technician course with the robot maker and asks the owners to pay half. Considers moving to the dealer to fix robots on farms across the area.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with a warning voice telling her not to get cocky.
S1.quote: The cows already work for a robot. Petr's the one who'd struggle to.
S1.fieldNote: Daria knows her advantage is temporary even in the moderate scenario, which is unusually self-aware. She'd follow the money to the robot dealer while treating her current employer fairly. She worries about a colleague who is good with calves but avoids screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, then it's a sprint. I'd stop thinking in careers and start thinking in months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say everyone needs to move now, not next year. I'd be honest that I don't know what's safe. I'd be sharing whatever useful info I found, which courses, which jobs are hiring, without pretending to have the answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the robot-fixing jobs would boom for about a year and then shrink when the robots learn to fix themselves. So I'd grab that year. In two years, being early is the only advantage left, and it lasts about twelve months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Move to the dealer as a technician straight away and work every hour they give me. Put a chunk of my savings into shares in the companies making the robots, because if they're taking the jobs, I want a slice of what they earn. Then save every spare bit of the higher wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Wired, like after too much coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying shares a risk with only five months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. I'd keep three months as cash and put the rest in. If I'm wrong, I've lost two months of bills. If I'm right, it might be the only thing that grows when wages don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to think about it too, because the lifting robots are already in some hospitals. She'd say I'm being dramatic. We'd argue a bit over dinner, then she'd ask me to send her the course links.

S2.say: I'd tell everyone to move now, not next year, while being honest that I don't know what's safe. I'd share useful information about courses and jobs without pretending to have answers.
S2.think: Robot-fixing jobs would boom for about a year before robots learn to fix themselves, so I'd grab that year. Being early is the only advantage left, and it lasts about twelve months.
S2.do: Moves straight to the robot dealer as a technician and works every hour offered. Keeps three months of savings as cash, puts the rest into shares in robot makers, and saves as much of the higher wage as she can.
S2.feel: Anxious and wired, like after too much coffee.
S2.quote: In two years, being early is the only advantage left, and it lasts about twelve months.
S2.fieldNote: Daria treats the fast scenario as a timing problem: grab the short boom in robot repair and buy a slice of the companies doing the replacing. Her centre outlook shows in owning shares rather than calling for public ownership. She keeps a cash buffer, so her risk-taking is measured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to build something, not just grab something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to get ready and to be practical about it. Learn the machines, save money, and think about what you'd do if you didn't need a job. That last bit sounds odd, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the people who come out okay are the ones who own something by the time it lands. A wage won't be enough. I'd want to be managing robots across several farms, as a business, not as an employee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the technician course in year one, then start a small herd data service on the side, checking the robot data for three or four farms who can't make sense of it. Put a bit of savings into shares each month, not a big lump. Leave the Brandts by year three if the side business is paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more in control. I like a five-year plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk with the side business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the AI gets good enough to read the data itself before my business is big enough to matter. I'm basically racing the thing I'm selling. But I'd rather race than stand still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change how you feel about Petr and the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because there's time to help. I'd sit with Petr for an hour a week and show him the calf app, if he'd let me. In two years there's no time for that. In five there is.

S3.say: I'd say it's time to get ready practically: learn the machines, save, and think about what you'd do if you didn't need a job. That last point sounds odd but I'd say it.
S3.think: People who own something by the time it lands will come out okay, because a wage won't be enough. I'd want to manage robots across several farms as a business, not an employee.
S3.do: Takes the technician course in year one and starts a side business reading robot data for three or four farms. Buys shares in small monthly amounts and plans to leave her employer by year three if the business pays.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more in control, steadied by a five-year plan.
S3.quote: I'm basically racing the thing I'm selling.
S3.fieldNote: Five years moves Daria from grabbing short-term pay to building ownership. She sees plainly that she's racing the AI she's selling, and accepts the race. Extra time also opens room to help her screen-shy colleague, which she couldn't do in the fast version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough that I might end up owning a farm, oddly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's not wait for it to be done to us. Every young farmer I know should be learning the kit and saving. And I'd say the government should make it easier for young people to get into farming as owners, not just workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, with ten years I'd aim to run my own small robotic dairy by 2036, renting the land and the robots. If almost all the work is robots, the money goes to whoever owns the cows and the kit. Ten years is long enough to stop being the worker and start being the owner. Two years isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save hard, a third of my wage, and do a part-time course in farm business management. Learn everything about the robots from the technician side for the first few years. Then, around year five or six, look for a retiring farmer willing to rent me a small unit, maybe even moving region for the right one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but properly hopeful. It's the one where I can picture my own life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything goes cheaper and only the giant farms survive. Or the land prices go silly. I'd watch it every year and if I saw it going that way, I'd switch to just owning shares instead of cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the warning time change things for you, across all three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I sprint and grab. Five, I build a side business. Ten, I might own the whole thing. For someone my age with a bit saved, time turns into ownership, and ownership is what matters when the work's gone.

S4.say: I'd say we have time, so let's not wait for it to be done to us. Young farmers should learn the kit and save, and the government should help young people become farm owners, not just workers.
S4.think: I'd aim to run my own small robotic dairy by 2036, renting the land and robots, because the money will go to whoever owns the cows and kit. Ten years is long enough to go from worker to owner, and two years isn't.
S4.do: Saves a third of her wage and takes a part-time farm business course while learning robots on the technical side. Around year five or six looks for a retiring farmer to rent her a small unit, even if it means moving region.
S4.feel: Uneasy but properly hopeful, because she can picture her own life.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to stop being the worker and start being the owner. Two years isn't.
S4.fieldNote: Daria gave the clearest account of how warning time turns into ownership for a young person with some savings. She has a backup plan of owning shares if land becomes unaffordable. The ten-year scenario is the only one in which she can picture her own future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to become an owner, so I'd just be a worker in a world that doesn't need workers. What would help is cheap loans for young people to rent land and robots, and honest information about which jobs are actually growing, not adverts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who'll own the farms in ten years. Everyone talks about jobs, but on a robot farm the question is who owns the robots and the cows. If it's only big companies, places like ours empty out.

headlineQuote: Ten years is long enough to stop being the worker and start being the owner. Two years isn't.
portrait: Daria is a 27-year-old junior on a 300-cow dairy that already milks with robots, sharing a house in town with a nurse friend. She's a practical centrist who uses AI tools every day for herd data, though she's still weaker than her colleagues at handling cows. She sees the plateau as today's normal and steady disruption as her chance to become a robot technician. Faced with AGI, she treats warning time as a route to ownership: sprint and grab with two years, build a side business with five, and aim to own a small robotic dairy with ten. She hedges each step with a cash buffer and shares in robot makers.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because there'd be no time to become an owner and she'd be a worker in a world that no longer needs workers.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for young people to rent land and robots, and honest information about which jobs are really growing.
